extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of Indian theatre and aesthetics (actors, directors, dramatists)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Bharata's Rasa theory describing how theatrical elements (vibhava, anubhava, vyabhichari, sattvika, sthayi) combine to produce aesthetic relish (rasa) in the spectator; aimed at guiding performers, directors and students in evoking rasa on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa Sutra (Vibhava–Anubhava–Vyabhichari-samyogad rasa nishpattih)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Vibhava-anubhava-vyabhichari-samyogad rasa nishpattih." The aesthetic relish (rasa) is produced by a combination of the determinants (vibhava), consequents (anubhava), and transitory states or fleeting emotions (vyabhicharibhava).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rasa is the essence derived from the various ingredients; like extracts of condiments becoming delectable when combined. To evoke rasa the performer must assemble appropriate determinants, consequents and transitory states in performance. This sutra is the central formula for composing dramatic emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model spectator (Sahrdaya) as necessary participant
rubrics_metrics.description: The model spectator is a Sahrdaya, someone 'who empathizes with the author.' The success of a performance is measured by whether or not the audience has a specific experience (rasa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers and producers should aim their craft at a sahrdaya: an audience capable of empathic relish. The spectator is a vital participant — evocation of rasa depends on the spectator's perception and cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bhava–Rasa interdependence (Bhava becomes Rasa)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bhava is the emotion represented in the performance; Rasa is the aesthetic relish experienced by the spectator. 'Bhava is that which becomes rasa.' Bhavas by themselves carry no meaning in the absence of Rasa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators must transform character-emotions (bhavas) into a form that produces rasa in the spectator. Attention to how bhava is staged (gestures, context) is essential because only through this transformation does rasa arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natya-rasa: stage representation (not literal reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natya Rasa is an aesthetic relish possible only through mental perception; vibhava, anubhava and vyabhicharibhava refer only to stage representations, not to realities of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both performers and spectators understand the enjoyment is aesthetic, not literal; performance techniques should foreground the awareness of representation (abhinaya) so that rasa is relished without confusing it with real-life feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal sequence: Vibhava → Bhava → Anubhava → Rasa
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional causation is formulated as: VIBHAVA—causes—>BHAVA—causes—>ANUBHAVA—>RASA. Vibhava (determinant) triggers Bhava (feeling), which manifests as Anubhava (physical/behavioral consequents) producing Rasa in the spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stagecraft should articulate determinants clearly (setting, stimuli), cultivate convincing inner bhava in performers, and execute precise anubhavas (actions, facial expressions, speech) so the causal chain reliably yields rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Vibhava: Alambana and Uddipana
rubrics_metrics.description: Vibhava (determinant) is of two types: Alambana Vibhava (the main stimulating cause) and Uddipana Vibhava (environmental/excitant factors that assist evocation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and stage the central cause (alambana) for the emotion and support it with atmospheric, temporal, social, or prop-based uddipana elements. Examples: time of year, presence of loved ones, decor, costume, music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anubhava: consequent physical/expressive manifestations
rubrics_metrics.description: Anubhava is the consequent physical reaction through action, word and facial expression that follows the vibhava; it is equipped with Vak (speech), Anga (physical), and Satva (inner quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anubhavas must be performed with integrated speech, body, and inner attitude. Examples include weeping, blushing, fainting, specific gestures and vocal changes; proper execution causes the audience to share the corresponding rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sthayi bhavas (durable, dominant emotions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sthayi bhavas are eight 'durable' or 'constant' emotional conditions (Rati, Hasa, Shoka, Krodha, Utsaha, Bhaya, Jugupsa, Vismaya) that are inherent and dominant in human behavior and form the basis for rasas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sthayi bhava is the stable core that attains 'rasa-hood'; performances should orient all other emotional ingredients to strengthen the dominant sthayi. Each sthayi has typical anubhavas (e.g., Rati: smiling eyes, sidelong glances; Shoka: shedding tears).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vyabhichari (Sanchari) bhavas: transitory states
rubrics_metrics.description: Vyabhichari bhavas are thirty-three transitory, fleeting emotional states (e.g., despondency, envy, recollection, anxiety, sleep, delirium) that arise and pass, and help in the evolution and strengthening of the sthayi bhava.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate fleeting emotions to colour and develop the dominant emotion; they appear in sequence to reinforce the sthayi until rasa is established. Note some listed vyabhicharis are situational (e.g., death) rather than pure emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sattvika bhavas: physiological manifestations of intense emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Sattvika bhavas are eight involuntary physical manifestations (stambha, sveda, romanca, svarabheda, vepathu, vaivarnya, asru, pralaya) resulting from intense inner emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sattvika abhinaya (gesticulation of temperamental states) is central: these subtle physiological signs must be convincingly produced (or simulated convincingly) to convey authenticity. Techniques include controlled breathing, voice change, simulated tremor, tears, color-change effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sattvika abhinaya importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperamental states are expressed on the stage using Sattvika abhinaya; Bharata gives prominence to gesticulation of temperament as necessary, otherwise the real purpose of performance would be lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors must cultivate the inner impulse that manifests as sattvika signs; mere external mimicry may appear artificial. Emphasize inner psychological cause to make physical manifestations believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical Rasas and their gestural/anubhava representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentiments (rasas) classically include: Sringara (love), Hasya (comic), Karuna (pathos), Roudra (furious), Veera (heroic), Bhayanaka (fear), Bibhatsa (disgust), Adbhuta (wonder); Shantha (tranquility) was later added as a ninth. Each rasa has prescribed anubhavas and gestural signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each rasa stage prescribed facial expressions, body language, vocal qualities and contextual indicators. Examples: Sringara in union—soft eye movements, delicate limbs; Karuna—shedding tears, drooping limbs; Bhaya—trembling, pallor, loss of voice; Adbhuta—wide eyes, horripilation. Use these codified signs to reliably evoke the intended rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hasya subdivisions and suitability by character type
rubrics_metrics.description: Hasya (comic) has six types: 'smita' (gentle smile), 'hasita' (smile), 'vihasita' (gentle laugher), 'upahasita' (laugher of ridicule), 'apahasita' (vulgar laugher), 'atihasita' (excessive laugher).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subtype appropriate to the character's social/type status: smita and hasita for superior characters, vihasita/upahasita for middling, apahasita/atihasita for inferior types. Each subtype has distinct facial and vocal anubhavas (e.g., teeth visibility, intensity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence: number of rasas ↔ number of sthayi bhavas
rubrics_metrics.description: Since it is the Sthayi which attains to Rasa-hood, the number of Rasas corresponds to the number of Sthayis. Bharata considers eight Rasas, though later writers expanded the list (Udbhata, Abhinavagupta).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the dominant sthayi to its rasa and design performance elements accordingly. Be aware of later additions (e.g., Shanta) when adapting or interpreting classical theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the director (Sutradhara) in conveying bhavas
rubrics_metrics.description: The director should properly understand the idea and bhavas of the character and convey his knowledge and understanding to the actors. Actors perform using their vision but should follow main ideas and key bhavas emphasized by the Sutradhara.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directorial responsibility includes choosing the dominant sthayi/rasa to be established, staging vibhavas, guiding actors' anubhavas and sattvika work, and ensuring coherence of the rasa experience across production elements (music, decor, pacing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor's role as bearer, medium and connector of emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor acts as bearer, media and connector of emotions: by conveying emotions the actor opens the inner Bhava-Jagat of the character and creates an emotional atmosphere for the spectators to relish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors must embody and transmit character-emotions step by step, using integrated vak/anga/satva; their work must invite collective sharing of rasa among the audience rather than mere individual display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasanubhaava and Rasotpatti: process of rasa formation and Siddhi
rubrics_metrics.description: Several emotions follow one after the other, strengthening the Sthayi at each stage until the dominant mood is established ('Rasanubhaava'). Performers/producers should be conscious of the Sthayi and Rasa they strive to establish to realize 'Siddhi' through 'Rasotpatti'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan sequences where transient emotions accumulate and support the dominant sthayi; monitor pacing and intensity so the audience's relish culminates in Siddhi (successful experience of rasa).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shanta rasa debate and Abhinavagupta's expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Natyashastra does not clearly recognize shanta, but Abhinavagupta expanded the rasa spectrum by adding Shantha (tranquility/peace) as a ninth rasa, interpreting rasa as a stream of consciousness and treating shanta as the summum bonum underlying other rasas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars and practitioners may include Shanta as an interpretive layer; productions aiming for spiritual/tranquil aesthetic should structure bhavas and anubhavas to culminate in a tranquil rasa rather than purely emotive ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natya as imitation of life and glorification of emotions (lokanukruti & bhavanukirtanam)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata says Natya is the imitation of life (lokanukruti) wherein various human emotions have to be dramatically glorified (bhavanukirtanam) so the spectator can 'flavour' the portrayed pleasure and pain as Natyarasa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic representation should amplify and stylize real-life emotions (not slavishly reproduce them) so that spectators can aesthetically relish the essence; use heightened gesture, concentrated situations and crafted dialogue to glorify emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa as aesthetic relish and spectator effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa is an aesthetically transformed emotional state experienced by the spectator, accompanied by feelings of pleasure and enjoyment; it tunes perception, creates empathy, and helps open mind and heart to the idea and message of the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure success of performance by the extent to which audience experiences empathic relish and cognitive/emotional openness. Design production elements (music, pacing, imagery) to produce pleasure and understanding rather than mere shock or sensation.
